analysis.one_liner: Taxed securities trades to fund public jobs in high-unemployment communities and job training.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the 111th Congress after being referred to two House committees in May 2010.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Full Employment National Trust Fund, financed by a new tax on securities transactions, capped at 0.25 percent of the value of each trade and paid by the trading facility. The money would fund grants to states, cities, and tribes to hire the long-term unemployed for community work — repairing schools, cleaning up vacant properties, staffing child care and food programs — plus additional funding for existing job training programs. Unemployment had to be above set thresholds (starting at 9 percent) for the grants to flow.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed people in high-unemployment communities, especially those out of work 26 weeks or more and low-income workers from targeted groups; also local governments, schools, and nonprofits that would receive grant-funded staff and improvements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The long-term unemployed in distressed communities

how_it_helps.text: Creates Employment Opportunity Grants for states, local governments, and Indian tribes to fund jobs in communities where unemployment exceeds set thresholds (9 percent in year one, stepping down to 4 percent after ten years).

Requires that at least 80 percent of project funding go to wages, benefits, and support services like child care, and that workers be paid no less than similar existing employees, with prevailing wages on construction work.

Targets workers who have been unemployed at least 26 weeks, or at least 30 days and low-income members of targeted groups, and bars grant-funded workers from displacing existing employees or replacing furloughed staff.
Reserves a third of the fund to finance programs under the Workforce Investment Act, the main federal job-training system.
Requires each grantee to run an outreach program in low-income communities so residents learn about the placements, and to consult labor organizations and local residents in planning projects.

analysis.who_pays: Securities and derivatives trading firms, which would pay the transaction tax at the trading facility; the industry would likely pass some of the cost to investors through higher trading costs.

drawbacks.text: The tax is paid by trading facilities, which can pass it to investors, so the cost would fall partly on ordinary savers and retirement accounts through higher transaction costs, and a tax on every trade can reduce market trading activity.

The tax rate is capped at 0.25 percent and sized to equal the Treasury's estimate of the net cost of the TARP bailout and related Federal Reserve lending, so the funding available depends on that estimate and could be smaller than the job programs require.

Deposit into the trust fund is subject to the availability of appropriations, and grants only flow if unemployment is above the statutory thresholds, so the program could be underfunded or dormant in better years.

In the first nine months, grants could only fund a short list of fast-track placements such as repairing schools, revitalizing vacant properties, expanding emergency food programs, and staffing early-childhood programs, limiting flexibility to match local needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directed real money to a genuine problem: in 2010, unemployment was near 10 percent and long-term unemployment was at record levels, and the bill required most funding to go to wages rather than administration, with wage floors and anti-displacement protections. The main cost is the transaction tax, which would raise trading costs for the financial sector and, in part, for ordinary investors; at a cap of 0.25 percent per trade the burden is modest per transaction but falls on the sector with the highest profits at the time. The design is relatively careful about not displacing existing jobs and prioritizing the highest-need areas, though its dependence on a TARP-cost estimate and on appropriations makes the funding uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees in May 2010, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on May 4, 2010, and it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On May 7, 2010, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Income Security and Family Support, and on May 27, 2010, to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
Only one member, all from the House Democratic caucus, cosponsored the bill.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was held, and no further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The securities and derivatives trading industry is better off because the transaction tax never advanced, while the long-term unemployed in high-unemployment communities received no jobs program from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The trading industry; no jobs program followed

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by George Miller, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on May 27, 2010, and took no further action; never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sander Levin, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Income Security and Family Support on May 7, 2010, and took no further action; never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; after subcommittee referral the bill sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were both House Democrats, and no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: The bill would tax each covered securities transaction, paid by the trading facility, at up to 0.25 percent of the trade's value, with proceeds funding the jobs trust fund. The industry's interest in blocking the tax ran against the public's interest in the jobs funding it would finance, and trading facilities would likely pass part of the cost to investors.

industries.industry: Public workforce training system (Workforce Investment Act providers)
industries.note: One-third of the trust fund would flow to programs under the Workforce Investment Act, locking in and enlarging the existing workforce system's funding. That funding would serve unemployed workers seeking training.

industries.industry: Local governments, schools, and nonprofits in distressed communities
industries.note: Grants would fund their staffing and projects — repairing schools, restoring vacant properties, expanding food and child-care programs — creating paid positions they could not otherwise fund.
